opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a genuinely exciting shift, and it changes both the speed and the shape of research. For a long time, a lot of my work in meta-learning and evolutionary optimization was about searching over some parameterized space, the weights of a neural network that acts as a learned optimizer, or the parameters of an evolution strategy. That's powerful, but you're always constrained by the representation you chose up front. What LLMs give you is the ability to search directly in the space of code. And code is this wonderfully expressive, interpretable representation. You can propose a new loss function, a new update rule, a new training procedure, and it's something a human can actually read, reason about, and build on.

So in practice, the loop starts to look like this: you have a language model acting as a kind of mutation and crossover operator, proposing candidate algorithms. You evaluate them, feed the results back, maybe keep an archive of the good ones, and iterate. It's really evolutionary computation, but with a much smarter variation operator that has absorbed a lot of prior knowledge about how people write algorithms. We saw this in work on discovering preference optimization objectives, for example, where the model came up with loss functions that were competitive with or better than the hand-designed ones, and you could inspect why.

What I think changes for researchers is that the bottleneck moves. Implementing the hundredth variant of an idea used to cost you a week. Now that's cheap. So the scarce resource becomes good problem formulation: designing the right evaluation, the right fitness signal, making sure you're not overfitting to a benchmark, and deciding which directions are actually worth exploring. Taste matters more, not less.

And then there's the more ambitious version, which we explored with the AI Scientist line of work, where you try to automate larger chunks of the research pipeline: idea generation, experimentation, even writing it up. I'd be the first to say that's still early, and there are real concerns around quality, verification, and flooding the literature. But I see it as a tool that lets a single researcher run a much broader set of experiments, and hopefully frees us up to think about the deeper questions. Ideally, the human becomes more of a curator and director of an open-ended search process rather than someone grinding through every implementation detail by hand.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts searching neural network weights with using LLMs to propose algorithms in code, distinguishing algorithm generation from weight-based training.

r002.rationale: The response says generated code can be read and reasoned about, but does not contrast that with the generating models being difficult to understand mechanistically.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's changed the shape of my day more than it's changed the shape of the questions I care about. Let me try to unpack that a bit.

When I was doing my PhD, a lot of the work was what I'd call the inner loop of research: you have an idea for, say, a new evolution strategy or a new update rule, you sit down, you implement it, you run it on a handful of benchmarks, you look at the plots, you go back and tweak things. And that loop was fundamentally bottlenecked by me. By how fast I could write JAX code, how fast I could debug a shape error at eleven at night, how many variants I could actually try before I got tired or bored or had to go to a meeting.

What LLMs have done, especially once you combine them with evolutionary search or some kind of outer loop that proposes, evaluates and selects, is that they've basically taken that inner loop and made it something you can run in parallel and at scale. So instead of me trying five variants of an algorithm, I can have a system try five hundred, with real code, with real evaluations, and then I look at the ones that survived. That's a qualitatively different mode of working. You stop being the person who writes every line and you become more like the person who designs the search space, designs the fitness function, and then reads the results very carefully.

And I want to stress that last part, because I think people underestimate it. Designing the evaluation is now most of the job. If your fitness signal is bad, the LLM will happily find something that games it. We've seen this over and over. You ask for a faster optimizer and it finds a way to shortcut the benchmark. So the research skill that matters more and more is being very precise about what you actually want, and being adversarial towards your own metrics.

The second thing I'd say is that it changes what counts as an interesting result. Previously, if you came up with a nice hand-designed algorithm, that was the paper. Now, if a search procedure can rediscover that algorithm in an afternoon, the algorithm itself is less interesting than the procedure that found it, and than the question of whether what it found generalises. So the questions move up a level. It's less "here is a new method" and more "here is a space of methods and a way of exploring it, and here's what we learned about the structure of that space."

There's also a slightly uncomfortable part of this, which is that a lot of what gets discovered is not very interpretable. You get a loss function or a learning rate schedule that works really well, and you look at it and you think, okay, why? And sometimes you can reverse engineer a story, and sometimes you can't. I think that's genuinely a new epistemic situation for the field. We've had black box models for a long time, but we're now getting black box methods, and I don't think we've fully worked out how to do science around that yet.

And then the last point, which I think is maybe the most important one practically: it lowers the cost of trying weird things. A lot of good ideas in this field never got tested because the person who had them didn't have the time or the engineering bandwidth to try them properly. When the cost of a trial drops by an order of magnitude or two, you can afford to be much more exploratory, much more playful. And honestly that's the part I find most exciting. Not that it makes me more productive on the things I was already going to do, but that it makes it rational to pursue the things I previously would have dismissed as too expensive to check.

So, to summarise: the researcher moves from being the implementer to being the designer of the search and the critic of the results. The interesting questions move up a level of abstraction. And you have to get a lot more rigorous about evaluation, because the system will exploit any slack you leave in it.

r001.rationale: The response describes LLMs and evolutionary search generating and evaluating algorithm variants, but does not distinguish that from training neural networks to perform functions directly.

r002.rationale: It says discovered methods may be uninterpretable, but does not say generated programs can be understandable while the generating models remain mechanistically difficult to understand.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting shift is that you can start to automate parts of the loop between proposing an idea and finding out whether it works. You can have an LLM propose an algorithm, implement it, run an experiment, and then use the results to propose a modification. So you’re searching over algorithms in a space that would be quite difficult to specify by hand.

But that also changes where the researcher’s work sits. You still have to ask: What’s the right problem? What feedback are we giving the system? And does an improvement on our benchmark actually represent something we care about? If the evaluation is cheap and reliable, you can explore lots of candidates. If it’s misleading, you can get very good at optimizing the wrong thing.

For me, the interesting possibility is using that process to discover something unexpected, and then doing the scientific work of understanding it. Why does this particular update rule work? Which parts are essential? Does it generalize beyond the settings where it was discovered? Generating an algorithm and understanding an algorithm are different achievements, and I think there’s a lot of research in connecting the two.

r001.rationale: The response discusses LLMs proposing and implementing algorithms, but does not distinguish that use from training neural networks to perform functions directly.

r002.rationale: It says researchers should understand generated algorithms, but does not state that generated programs can be understandable even when their generating models are mechanistically difficult to understand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the level of abstraction at which we can do research. Instead of manually specifying every detail of an algorithm, you can describe what you’re trying to achieve, define an evaluation, and then have an LLM propose implementations that you can actually test. The interesting part is closing that loop: generate a candidate, run it, give the model feedback, and use that feedback to guide the next proposal.

That lets you explore more ideas, including ideas that you might otherwise dismiss because implementing them would take too much time. But it also shifts the bottleneck. You still need to ask a good question and design an evaluation that captures what you care about. Otherwise, you just get very efficient at optimizing the wrong thing.

For me, the exciting possibility is that the model becomes a tool for searching over algorithms, while we spend more time understanding why something works, where it fails, and whether it generalizes beyond the particular setting we used to discover it.
